chunks: Ḥammād narrated from al-Ḥalabī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, that he said:

Regarding a man to whom a woman entrusted her affair—whether a relative or a neighbor—and he did not know the hidden reality of her condition, then he found that she had concealed a defect that was in her, he said: “The mahr is taken from her, and there is nothing upon the one who married her off.”

And he said concerning a woman who entrusted her affair to a man and said, “Marry me to so-and-so.” He said, “I will not marry you until you testify that your affair is in my hand.” So she testified for him. Then at the time of the marriage contract he said to the one proposing to her, “O so-and-so, upon you is such-and-such and such-and-such.” He said, “Yes.” Then he said to the people, “Bear witness that that is due to her from me, and I have married her to myself.” So the woman said, “I would never marry you—no honor at all—and my affair is only in my own hand. I only entrusted you with my affair out of modesty in speech.” He said: “She is removed from him, and his head is to be struck.”

key_terms.تُنْزَعُ: she is separated or removed from him
key_terms.دَخِيلَةَ: the hidden reality or inner state of a matter
key_terms.دَلَّسَتْ: she concealed or fraudulently hid a defect
key_terms.عَيْبًا: a defect affecting the marriage case
key_terms.وَلَّتْهُ: she entrusted him with authority over her affair

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a marriage agent is deceived by a woman’s concealed defect or unlawfully marries her to himself?
ai.summary: This hadith addresses legal rulings related to agency in marriage and the consequences of deception. It states that if a woman conceals a defect, the mahr may be recovered from her, and an unwitting agent is not liable; it also condemns a fraudulent agent who marries the woman to himself without her true consent.
